clinical_background: Allergic rhinitis is commonly managed with intranasal or oral medications. Current guidelines, such as ARIA 2020, suggest intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe disease, citing faster onset and higher effectiveness, but the certainty of evidence for these recommendations is often low or very low. Similarly, the US 2020 Practice Parameter recommends intranasal corticosteroids as first-line therapy without detailed comparisons with oral options. Existing head-to-head studies have employed heterogeneous outcome measures and inconsistent methodological rigor. Recent high-quality systematic reviews on this topic are absent; the last comprehensive review was published in 1998 and limited to intranasal corticosteroids versus oral antihistamines, while a later review imposed language and date restrictions. An updated evidence synthesis is required to support the 2024 revision of the ARIA guidelines.
objectives: To conduct a systematic review and meta-analysis comparing the effectiveness of intranasal corticosteroids or intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists in improving nasal and ocular symptoms and quality of life in allergic rhinitis.
To assess the safety of these interventions by evaluating adverse events and withdrawals due to adverse events.
clinical_question: In patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis (P), how do intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) (I) compare with oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists) (C) in improving total nasal symptom score, total ocular symptom score, and rhinoconjunctivitis quality of life (O)?
interpretation: The meta-analysis found that intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) or intranasal antihistamines (INAH) are more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) or leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) in improving nasal and ocular symptoms in seasonal allergic rhinitis (SAR), as well as quality of life. Most effects were considered clinically relevant. Safety outcomes were generally similar between intranasal and oral treatments, except for a higher risk of adverse events with INAH compared to OAH. The certainty of evidence (CoE) for most comparisons was moderate or high, supporting the reliability of these findings.
comparison_with_prior_evidence: Previous systematic reviews on this topic were older, assessed fewer drug classes, and restricted study selection based on publication dates or languages. They did not use the GRADE approach to evaluate CoE. However, their results consistently suggested superiority of intranasal over oral medications, aligning with the current findings.
clinical_implications: These results reinforce current ARIA Guidelines and the US Practice Parameter recommendations that favor intranasal treatments for moderate-to-severe allergic rhinitis, though they should be considered alongside other evidence.
The findings support clinically meaningful improvements with intranasal treatments over oral medications, which could guide shared decision-making between clinicians and patients.

Patient preferences, disease severity, and real-world usage patterns (e.g., over-the-counter oral medication use) must be weighed when applying these findings, as most clinical trial participants may have more severe disease than typical patients.
practice_implications: Despite the demonstrated superiority of intranasal treatments, factors such as cost, ease of use, and patient preference may lead to continued prescribing or self-medication with oral agents.
Clinicians should consider the comparative effectiveness evidence when selecting between intranasal and oral medications, but also integrate patient-centered aspects in treatment decisions.
limitations: Insufficient evidence on perennial allergic rhinitis (PAR) limited the ability to perform meta-analyses for this condition, so findings chiefly apply to SAR.
Only a minority of included studies had a low risk of bias; most had unclear risk, and some had high risk, potentially biasing results.

Considerable heterogeneity existed in outcome measurement: some studies used nonstandard definitions of TNSS (e.g., 3 or 5 symptoms) or TOSS (2 or 4 symptoms), and the Total Symptom Score (TSS) could not be meta-analyzed due to inconsistent definitions.
Missing spread measures in several studies required imputation based on P values, though sensitivity analyses excluding such studies yielded consistent findings.
The inability to comprehensively assess the effect of individual drugs within each class, due to the low number of studies per comparison, could mask variability in effectiveness.
The overall comparison between intranasal and oral treatments might be influenced by class-specific differences in effectiveness and safety, as well as the proportion of studies assessing each class.
The classification of rhinitis as seasonal/perennial rather than intermittent/persistent reflects the design of included RCTs, though the authors believe results may generalize.
strengths: The systematic review used an extensive search of four bibliographic databases and three clinical trial registries, without restrictions on language, date, or publication status, minimizing publication bias.
The GRADE approach was applied to assess certainty of evidence for each outcome across comparisons.
Sensitivity analyses were conducted examining risk of bias, imputation of spread measures, follow-up duration, and individual drugs compared.
When potential effect modification was identified, the credibility of that modification was assessed using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses (ICEMAN).
A complementary method was used to evaluate the probability that observed differences corresponded to clinically relevant effects, based on decision thresholds.
open_questions: The effectiveness of intranasal versus oral treatments for perennial allergic rhinitis remains uncertain due to insufficient data.
Whether the results apply equally to intermittent and persistent AR, using modern classification, needs confirmation through further research.
The variability in effectiveness among individual drugs within the same class was not fully addressed.
future_directions: Future RCTs and observational studies should use standardized outcomes, such as the four-symptom TNSS, three-symptom TOSS, and RQLQ, to ensure comparability.
More evidence is needed for PAR, either from RCTs or real-world data, to validate the transportability of findings from SAR trials.
Research employing real-world data and modern causal inference methods could better inform the comparative effectiveness and safety of treatments for intermittent and persistent allergic rhinitis.

study_design: Systematic review with meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials.

population.description: Patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal allergic rhinitis or perennial allergic rhinitis.
inclusion_criteria: Randomized controlled trials with a parallel design.
Patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal or perennial allergic rhinitis.

Comparison of intranasal medications (intranasal corticosteroids, intranasal antihistamines, or fixed combinations of intranasal corticosteroids plus intranasal antihistamines) versus oral medications (oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists).

Studies reporting at least one of the following patient-reported outcome measures: Total Nasal Symptom Score, Total Ocular Symptom Score, Total Symptom Score, or Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire.
Follow-up duration of at least 2 weeks for seasonal allergic rhinitis and at least 4 weeks for perennial allergic rhinitis.

interventions: Fixed combinations of INCS plus INAH
statistical_methods: Random-effects meta-analyses of mean differences in change from baseline were performed for effectiveness outcomes. Restricted maximum likelihood was used to estimate between-study variance. Heterogeneity was assessed using the Q-Cochran test P value and the I² statistic. Sensitivity analyses were conducted, including exclusion of studies with high risk of bias, imputed standard deviations, or non-2-week follow-up; and analyses restricted to specific drug comparisons. The credibility of effect modification in subgroup analyses was evaluated using the Instrument to Assess the Credibility of Effect Modification Analyses. A complementary approach computed probabilities of large, moderate, small, or trivial clinically relevant effects. Safety outcomes were meta-analyzed using risk ratios from random-effects models. Certainty of evidence was assessed with the GRADE approach.
follow_up: At least 2 weeks for seasonal allergic rhinitis and at least 4 weeks for perennial allergic rhinitis, based on inclusion criteria.
search_strategy: A systematic search was conducted in MEDLINE, Embase, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials from database inception to August 2022, with an updated search in September 2023. Manual searches were performed on clinicaltrials.gov, the GlaxoSmithKline clinical study dataset, and the AstraZeneca Clinical Trials website. No restrictions were applied based on publication language, date, or status.
databases: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials
quality_assessment_tool: Cochrane Risk of Bias tool for individual studies and GRADE for certainty of evidence.

tables.summary: Table shows key characteristics of included randomized controlled trials comparing intranasal versus oral treatments for allergic rhinitis. Studies assessed seasonal allergic rhinitis, with outcomes including TNSS, TOSS, RQLQ, and TSS. Follow-up ranged from 2 to 4 weeks. The most common intranasal treatments were azelastine, fluticasone propionate, fluticasone furoate, and budesonide; oral treatments included cetirizine, loratadine, fexofenadine, desloratadine, montelukast, and chlorpheniramine. Risk of bias was predominantly unclear due to poor reporting of randomization and allocation concealment; a few studies were at high risk of bias, mainly from selective reporting. Only the most representative rows are shown here; the full table contains 35 studies.

main_conclusion: Evidence from randomized controlled trials indicates that intranasal medications—corticosteroids or antihistamines—are more effective than oral antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists for reducing nasal and ocular symptoms and improving quality of life in seasonal allergic rhinitis, with a similar overall safety profile.
narrative_summary: This systematic review with meta-analysis synthesized data from 35 randomized controlled trials enrolling patients aged 12 years and older with seasonal allergic rhinitis. The review compared intranasal treatments (corticosteroids or antihistamines) against oral treatments (antihistamines or leukotriene receptor antagonists). Outcomes included Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS), Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS), Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ), adverse events, and withdrawals due to adverse events. Meta-analyses demonstrated that intranasal corticosteroids were significantly more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.86; 95% CI −1.21 to −0.51; I² = 70%), TOSS (MD −0.36; 95% CI −0.56 to −0.17; I² = 0%), and RQLQ (MD −0.88; 95% CI −1.15 to −0.61; I² = 0%). Intranasal corticosteroids also outperformed leukotriene receptor antagonists (TNSS MD −1.05; 95% CI −1.33 to −0.77). Intranasal antihistamines were more effective than oral antihistamines for TNSS (MD −0.47; 95% CI −0.81 to −0.14; I² = 0%) and RQLQ (MD −0.31; 95% CI −0.57 to −0.06; I² = 0%). Safety outcomes showed no significant differences between intranasal and oral treatments overall, except for a higher risk of adverse events with intranasal antihistamines versus oral antihistamines (RR 2.10; 95% CI 1.04–4.26). The certainty of evidence was moderate to high for most comparisons. These findings strongly support the preferential use of intranasal medications as first-line therapy for seasonal allergic rhinitis and may inform future guideline recommendations. However, the evidence is limited to seasonal allergic rhinitis; data on perennial disease are sparse.

main_findings.description: Intranasal treatments overall were more effective than oral treatments at improving the Total Nasal Symptom Score (TNSS) in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=65%, moderate certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 70%, based on 20 studies (6,742 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) were more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) at improving the TNSS in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=70%, low certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 68%, based on 15 studies (4,423 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) were more effective than oral leukotriene receptor antagonists (LTRA) at improving the TNSS in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=0%, high certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 98%, based on 2 studies (1,441 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal antihistamines (INAH) were more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) at improving the TNSS in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=0%, high certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 44%, based on 3 studies (878 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) were more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) at improving the Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS) in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=0%, high certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 21%, based on 5 studies (2,051 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal treatments overall were more effective than oral treatments at improving the Rhinoconjunctivitis Quality of Life Questionnaire (RQLQ) score in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=68%, high certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of moderate improvement 28% and small improvement 59%, based on 4 studies (1,022 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal corticosteroids (INCS) were more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) at improving the RQLQ score in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=0%, high certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of large improvement 72% and moderate improvement 28%, based on 2 studies (361 participants).

main_findings.description: Intranasal antihistamines (INAH) were more effective than oral antihistamines (OAH) at improving the RQLQ score in seasonal allergic rhinitis.
main_findings.context: I²=0%, low certainty of evidence (GRADE), probability of clinically relevant improvement 81%, based on 2 studies (661 participants).

safety_results.overall_adverse_events: No significant difference in risk of any adverse event between intranasal and oral treatments overall (RR 1.02, 95% CI 0.94-1.09, I²=0%, 22 studies, 6,520 participants, moderate certainty of evidence).
safety_results.discontinuations: No significant difference in risk of withdrawals due to adverse events (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.72-1.38, I²=0%, 30 studies, 8,792 participants, moderate certainty of evidence).
notable_adverse_events: Intranasal antihistamines (INAH) were associated with a higher risk of adverse events compared to oral antihistamines (OAH) (RR 2.10, 95% CI 1.04-4.26, I²=0%, low certainty of evidence).
Two serious adverse events were reported with intranasal corticosteroids and five with oral antihistamines, all unlikely to be related to treatment.

subgroup_analyses: Sensitivity analyses excluding studies with high risk of bias: INCS vs OAH for TNSS, MD -0.72 (95% CI -1.07 to -0.36, I²=73%), credibility of effect modification moderate; overall intranasal vs oral for TNSS, MD -0.70 (95% CI -0.98 to -0.44, I²=67%), credibility low.
Sensitivity analyses excluding studies with imputed standard deviations yielded consistent results for all comparisons.
Sensitivity analyses restricting to studies with 2-week follow-up also produced consistent findings.
Individual drug comparisons within classes (e.g., specific INCS vs specific OAH) are reported in online supplementary tables.
Subgroup analysis for perennial allergic rhinitis was not feasible due to insufficient data (only 2 studies with heterogeneous outcomes).
secondary_results: Meta-analysis of Total Symptom Score (TSS) was not possible because of substantial heterogeneity in the definition and included symptoms across studies.
No meta-analysis was performed for perennial allergic rhinitis due to only two studies reporting TSS with different definitions.

For all effectiveness outcomes, intranasal treatments demonstrated superiority, with the magnitude of effect varying by drug class: largest difference for INCS vs LTRA, followed by INCS vs OAH, and smallest for INAH vs OAH.
Probability analyses based on decision thresholds indicated that most comparisons had high probabilities of clinically relevant improvement, except for TOSS (21%) and INAH vs OAH for TNSS (44%).

scales_and_classifications.name: Total Ocular Symptom Score (TOSS)

scales_and_classifications.description: Questionnaire measuring quality of life in rhinoconjunctivitis; higher score indicates greater impairment.
